title: How do you handle adding 'juice' to your games with AI?
author: spartagon123
selftext:
I've built a puzzle game and I'm working on adding 'juice': "the extra visual, audio, and haptic feedback layered onto core mechanics to make actions feel more responsive, impactful, and satisfying".

I'm not new to software development, but I am to game development, and this is a new area for me. 

I find that this particular process is very trial and error... and just going back and forth with the AI output is taking a ton of iterations. I'm wondering if there are better tools or workflows for this than me just constantly saying things like...   
  
"try more color"   
"try making the text move faster"   
"try adding cool sounds" 

I feel like there's got to be a better way. Appreciate any help.

comments.author: delicious_pubes
comments.body: What kind of puzzle game? If it’s generic mobile slop then literally asking for a “juice” pass gives a lot. Lots of peggle learnings in there. Otherwise you can google articles or GDC talks on juice and game feel.

replies.author: spartagon123
replies.body:
I guess I'm mainly asking about the AI workflow... Like, I want it to be polished and according to my ideas and preferences... not just slop. But this process seems really slow of just iterating and trying different things. 

I'm wondering if there's like tools out there for mocking things up well, and seeing different options side by side, or provides better inspirations etc.

comments.author: Kingnorik
comments.body: I play other games in the genre and keep track about what I like about them. Then I let AI try to diagnose these games blindly and compare it to mine. Then I give it the reasons why I like it and we work from there to come up with a plan.

replies.author: spartagon123
replies.body: How do you do that comparison? Do you feed your AI a video of the gameplay? I'm not sure how well AI does with video... haven't experimented with that before

replies.author: Kingnorik
replies.body: My AI is the "lead programmer" of my game so it plays it and knows it well. AI's see videos as frame grabs. So a video does help. For the other games I just tell it to look them up.

replies.author: spartagon123
replies.body: How are you getting the AI to 'see' and play your game? Are you using a Chrome extension or what?

replies.author: Kingnorik
replies.body: Oh I work inside inside a game engine. Just sign into it with my subscription.  Check my profile.

replies.author: lgastako
replies.body: I'm not the person you're replying to, but I use Godot with the MCP which lets it take screenshots and also inspect the running state of the game.

comments.author: Kindly-Sail6260
comments.body:
Play test your game. Play it until you get tired of it. As you play your game you’ll start notice what your game might need in terms of juice. Seeing the result and iterating on it isn’t useful for feedback since you can’t make an informed decision as to what your game needs because it’s based on what you feel, not on what you see. 

So be a master of that game, have the discipline to play it (you will get bored of it eventually) and then make those changes.

comments.author: sillygoofygooose
comments.body: If you don't want to iterate a lot - specify what you actually want the output to be.

replies.author: spartagon123
replies.body: I guess that's the problem. When it comes to game mechanics, I can spend a lot of time thinking about what I want and decide.... when it comes to the animation and art... I kind of need to see it to decide if I like it or if that's the right direction... It's just really slow to ask AI for one change at a time...

replies.author: sillygoofygooose
replies.body: thumbnail it out. Google some juice animation patterns if you'd rather - there's a ton of existing methods for this. Sketch out what you want, then specify it to your agent using timings and keyframes, or upload an image of your thumbnails.

comments.author: Chinpara
comments.body:
参考の見た目があるなら動画をコマ撮りで真似させる  
それでもクオリティのための反復は必要だよ

comments.author: Xieboid
comments.body:
Trial and error and a ton of iterations is normal. Juice is hard to get right, but it's a differentiator, so good on you for investing in it. 

One thing you could try is describing the feeling you're trying to invoke, and ask your agent for some suggestions on how to achieve it.

replies.author: spartagon123
replies.body: Hm that's a good idea. Though I don't expect AI to be too good at 'feelings' haha. I'll give it a try

replies.author: Xieboid
replies.body: Haha, yeah. As always you need to make the judgement calls and verify the output, and there'll still be a lot of iterating.

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body: I downloaded the Feel pack for Unity, then told Claude to add juice to my game. It worked.

comments.author: velocimposter
comments.body:
Nope.  Experience and iteration.

Invoking a feeling isn't something you just make, it's a subjective human thing that you must feel out.  It's also a skill that you build up over time by failing and leaning.

If you are lost I'd suggest you first understood what juice is, how it works, why it works, what sort of juice have other games used in a similar genre.  Understand what is the feeling you want to invoke.  AI isn't going to fill those gaps for you, you must decide that for yourself.

comments.author: Vegetable_Voice_2044
comments.body:
Usually I play other games in the genre and go "oh that's cool, I wish my game did that! Hey Claude make the camera pan back when we engage the boosters and add those cool air streamers to the edge of the screen like this game does!".
Then I try another game in the genre and look for other such features I don't have in mine... Not everything makes the cut though, as I don't want every feature I seem but some stuff is just too good not to imitate.

comments.author: HouseOfWyrd
comments.body:
You work out exactly what you want to add and prompt accordingly.

AI shouldn't be making creative decisions for you. It's not fantastic at it.

comments.author: lgastako
comments.body:
Sometimes I have a specific idea, in which case I just code it like anything else.  If I don't...

I have a skill called "top3" which tells the AI to give me it's 3 best ideas for improving the application (game in this case).  You pass extra information after the skill invocation it takes that as an area to focus on.  The skill spits out it's top 3 suggestions and a suggested order.  So I invoke "/top3 juice" and then say "implement #1 please",  or "implement all three in order" or something along those lines.

comments.author: TheLastNeonDev
comments.body: trial and error is pretty normal i think. what helped me was playtests more than prompts, i just play it and send screenshots of whats off

comments.author: Any-Blacksmith-2054
comments.body: Thanks for haptic feedback idea. Forgot about it

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
this is in the design, UI/UX territory and technical devs would obviously struggle since we would be out of our elements. I have the same issue

the easiest way is probably just copying from other games and make sure your game have what they have i.e. camera shake or whatever else

I think you just need better understanding of design and thats it. it is not a technical challenge

comments.author: TheHabeo
comments.body:
Pick a style, make gpt or gemini do a few concept art and gauge your preference.

From the concept art you most of the time can also feel the sound and music that suits it.
